newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right slams govt over Thomson-CSF.
newsitem.headline: French right slams govt over Thomson-CSF.

text.p: France's right-wing opposition said on Saturday the Socialist-led government's decision to halt the sale of electronics firm Thomson-CSF was an "historic error" that would relegate France to the minor league of Europe's defence industry.

Francois Fillon, technology minister in the previous centre-right government that launched the Thomson-CSF privatisation last year, said the sale of the government's 58 percent stake was strategically important.
"(Prime Minister) Lionel Jospin is committing an error, an historic error, for which he will be accountable to the French people," Fillon told Europe 1 radio.
The trend was towards defence industry alliances in Europe to meet competition from a heavily restructured U.S. industry, strengthened by a series of massive mergers, he said.
"As for us, we choose to turn in on ourselves and force Thomson to play in the second division."
He said the state, now battling to reduce its deficits to qualify for a European single currency, lacked the resources to invest in Thomson-CSF's growth.

Jospin's government announced on Friday, six weeks after being elected, that it had halted the privatisation and would propose an alternative solution for a French defence electronics conglomerate based on the company.
The government said it would keep a "decisive" public stake in Thomson-CSF but did not say how big such a share might be.

A spokesman for Jospin declined to comment on a newspaper report that the government might still forge a partnership between Thomson-CSF and engineering giant Alcatel Alsthom, one of two groups which had bid to buy the firm outright.
The spokesman said no final decisions had been taken.

The report in Le Figaro said Jospin was leaning towards sharing out Thomson-CSF between a public stake of some 40 percent, another 20 percent remaining on the stock exchange and the rest dominated by Alcatel with its partner Dassault, the private French warplane manufacturer.

Afternoon daily Le Monde said the government would not sell its own stock in Thomson-CSF but had not ruled out seeing its percentage share in the company reduced below 50 percent through expansion of its capital or creation of a new joint entity.

Fillon hinted conservative President Jacques Chirac, who wants Thomson-CSF to be the French champion in a restructured defence industry, could intervene in the debate when he gives a traditional Bastille Day television interview on Monday.
Thomson-CSF, which makes radar, missiles and avionics, is seen as a vital part of European defence industry consolidation triggered by defence spending cuts and rapid U.S. concentration.
It had 1996 sales of 36.3 billion francs ($6.03 billion).

Le Monde quoted Jospin aides as saying the government had not yet decided whether to allow alliances between Thomson-CSF and other European defence firms at the same time as fixing its new structure or at some later stage.
Britain's GEC Plc has been tipped as a future industrial partner.
Right-wing Gaullist party spokesman Nicolas Sarkozy warned such alliances might now go ahead without France's involvement.

But the Communist party daily l'Humanite warmly praised the decision to halt the sale as "a breath of fresh air" proving the government was ready to honour electoral pledges. The Communists are junior partners in Jospin's "pink-red-green" coalition. ($1 = 6.02 francs)
